abstract: |
  The social media platform TikTok has surged in societal and political significance, underscoring the need for communication researchers to study its content and dynamics.
  `traktok` is an `R` package that combines an implementation of the TikTok Research API with access to TikTok content through web-scraping.
  While it is neither the first nor only tool to do so, the combination of both ways to retrieve data from the platform with an easy-to-understand consistent syntax is built to encourage TikTok research.
  The package enables searching for videos, retrieving user information, downloading video and image files, and collecting comments and follower networks.
  Importantly, both access methods can be combined, for example by using the Research API to identify relevant content and web-scraping to download the actual video files, enabling comprehensive data collection.
  An empirical comparison of both data access methods reveals significant discrepancies in data completeness, with both APIs returning different subsets of content, highlighting the importance of methodological transparency in TikTok research.
  The package has already been employed in several published studies across communication research and other disciplines, demonstrating its utility for systematic investigation of the platform.
acknowledgements: |
  `traktok` started out in 2022 as an `R` translation of Deen Freelon's pyktok Python module, and although all of its code has since been rewritten, I am grateful for this initial inspiration.
  I thank Miriam Milzner for help with testing the package.
  Much of the development around the Research API took place within the NEWSFLOWS project, which has received funding from the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme (Grant agreement No. 947695), and I thank Damian Trilling for giving me the freedom to pursue this side project.
  Finally, I thank everyone who has told me that they use `traktok` in their research and teaching: knowing that the package is useful to others is what keeps me developing and maintaining it.
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(traktok)
options(width = 70)

# Most code in this paper queries TikTok, which takes long and, for the
# 'hidden' API, sometimes needs a human to solve a CAPTCHA. The functions that
# contact TikTok are therefore replaced by versions that store their result in
# data/cache/ and only contact TikTok if no result for the same arguments is
# stored there yet. Delete data/cache/ to collect everything anew (authenticate
# once with auth_research() and auth_hidden() before, see the chunks below).
dir.create("data/cache", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
cache_dir <- here::here("data/cache")
the <- utils::getFromNamespace("the", "traktok")
cached <- function(fun_name) {
  fun <- getExportedValue("traktok", fun_name)
  function(...) {
    f <- file.path(
      cache_dir,
      paste0(fun_name, "_", rlang::hash(list(...)), ".rds")
    )
    if (!file.exists(f)) {
      value <- fun(...)
      saveRDS(
        list(value = value, videos = the$videos, comments = the$comments),
        f
      )
    }
    res <- readRDS(f)
    # restore what last_query() and last_comments() return after the call
    the$videos <- res$videos
    the$comments <- res$comments
    res$value
  }
}
for (fun_name in c(
  "tt_query_videos",
  "tt_search_api",
  "tt_comments_api",
  "tt_user_follower_api",
  "tt_user_following_api",
  "tt_search_hidden",
  "tt_user_info_hidden",
  "tt_get_following_hidden",
  "tt_videos",
  "tt_videos_hidden",
  "tt_request_hidden",
  "tt_user_videos_api",
  "tt_user_videos_hidden"
)) {
  assign(fun_name, cached(fun_name))
}

# all following chunks run inside data/, so the files traktok downloads
# (videos, images and its own json caches) end up there as well
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath("data"))
```

Since the social media platform TikTok went live in Europe in August 2018^[[https://www.theverge.com/2018/8/2/17644260/musically-rebrand-tiktok-bytedance-douyin](https://web.archive.org/web/20231122151117/https://www.theverge.com/2018/8/2/17644260/musically-rebrand-tiktok-bytedance-douyin)], it has quickly become one of the major players on the market.
As of early 2023, TikTok claims to have around 150 million users^[[https://newsroom.tiktok.com/en-eu/investing-for-our-150-m-strong-community-in-europe](https://web.archive.org/web/20231117185422/https://newsroom.tiktok.com/en-eu/investing-for-our-150-m-strong-community-in-europe)], many of whom are young and committed to the platform.
For instance, @newman_reuters_2023 positions TikTok as the third most-used platform among 18-24 year olds.
By 2026, over half of them use TikTok weekly and 36% use it for news, second only to Instagram in this age group [@egan_reuters_2026].^[The 2024 and 2025 editions of the Digital News Report do not report platform use among 18-24 year olds in this form.]
Given this reach, it is not surprising that the platform's content has been linked to a number of societal shifts, and the examples that make the headlines are mostly worrying ones: the increasing support for far-right parties among young voters in recent elections [@tjaden_does_2025]^[[https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/10/world/europe/germany-afd-eu-election.html](https://web.archive.org/web/20241003023927/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/06/10/world/europe/germany-afd-eu-election.html)], an anti-feminist backlash [@bauer_beauty_2024] or the rise of the 'manosphere' [@dhoest_manosphere_2025].
But TikTok is also where established political parties campaign [@widholm_right-wing_2024], where news organizations try to reach a young audience [@wirz_infotainment_2025], and where activists and ordinary users discuss and negotiate progressive norms around racism, sexism and homophobia [@peterson-salahuddin_teachable_2025].
Which of these developments dominates, for whom and under what circumstances, is an empirical question, and the purpose of `traktok` is to help communication researchers answer it based on systematic data rather than on the anecdotes that make the news.

Despite TikTok's significant influence, Communication Research has only begun to explore its unique affordances, particularly its combination of video-centric content and algorithmically driven user feeds [@boeker_empirical_2022].
These affordances have consequences: compared to YouTube, a larger share of TikTok users upload videos themselves, views depend less on an account's number of followers and more on going viral, and attention is spread more unevenly across the videos of the same account, which changes the incentives of who produces (political) content and how [@guinaudeau_fifteen_2022].
Initial research has examined how users discuss political issues with each other, finding interesting new dynamic forms of political discourse in duets between partisan users [@medina_serrano_dancing_2020], and its utilization in political campaigns, where candidates as of recently still failed to capitalize on the platform’s unique affordances [@cervi_tiktok_2023].
Some of the content is also genuinely new to political communication: @munger_thirst_2025 study 'edits' --- highly edited compilations of existing footage of politicians, set to music, where facticity is beside the point and the goal is to make the politician look attractive or impressive --- and show experimentally that these videos shift how voters evaluate them.
What these studies have in common is that their data were limited by what could be collected at the time rather than by their research questions.
@medina_serrano_dancing_2020 and @munger_thirst_2025 had to rely on TikTok's hashtag search, which returns an undisclosed selection of popular and recent videos, and the `R` package with which @guinaudeau_fifteen_2022 collected close to two million videos stopped working after TikTok implemented an update in late 2020.

Research challenges stem from both the computational complexity of analysing video content at scale --- which I will not address here --- and limited data access.
As @cervi_tiktok_2023 note, they had to search and collect posts manually, since any official API access was not available at the time.
While TikTok's 2023 introduction of a Research API has improved this situation by providing qualified researchers with platform access, they do not provide tools to work with the API directly and the access remains both selective and limited in scope.
Most prominently, it is still not possible to download images and videos from the platform.
Yet the video files are worth the effort: @kim_going_2023, for example, find that users engage differently with emotional and identity cues in anti-vaccination videos depending on whether these appear in the caption, the spoken audio, or the visuals, so that an analysis of textual metadata alone would miss an important part of how content on the platform works.
This creates a significant barrier for communication researchers who might possess deep theoretical knowledge and extensive experience studying other platforms, but lack the technical programming skills required to directly interface with REST APIs or implement web-scraping techniques.
Without accessible tools, these researchers --- despite their substantive expertise --- are effectively excluded from studying one of the most influential platforms for youth political engagement and information consumption.

Here I introduce `traktok`, an `R` package that combines an implementation of the TikTok Research API with access to TikTok content through web-scraping and the 'hidden' API, which was reverse engineered to grant users access to more content.
The tool works best for projects where researchers have access to the Research API, as the content delivered through the API can be enriched with the other functions.
However, even without Research API access, the package enables meaningful data collection through alternative methods.
By implementing both pathways to TikTok data in a single package, `traktok` also enables researchers to seamlessly perform audits of both data access strategies against each other, where functions are available for both pathways --- the official and unofficial.

@tbl-overview gives an overview of all functions in the package.
Since some functions are available for the Research API *and* the 'hidden' API, `traktok` offers some shorthand functions that automatically choose the Research API function in the background if credentials are available.
The following two sections detail the package's functions, categorized by their use of either the Research API or the scraping techniques, dubbed the 'hidden' API.
I then showcase how both paths can be combined meaningfully to gather insights into the platform's content and the shortcomings of the API TikTok offers to researchers at the moment.

| Description                 | Shorthand        | Research API              | 'Hidden' API              |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------|:--------------------------|:------------------------|
| search videos               | tt_search        | tt_search_api             | tt_search_hidden        |
| get video detail (+file)    | tt_videos        | \-                        | tt_videos_hidden        |
| get user videos             | tt_user_videos   | tt_user_videos_api        | tt_user_videos_hidden   |
| get user info               | tt_user_info     | tt_user_info_api          | tt_user_info_hidden     |
| get comments under a video  | tt_comments      | tt_comments_api           | \-                      |
| get who follows a user      | tt_get_follower  | tt_user_follower_api      | tt_get_follower_hidden  |
| get who a user is following | tt_get_following | tt_user_following_api     | tt_get_following_hidden |
| get videos a user liked     | tt_get_liked     | tt_user_liked_videos_api  | \-                      |
| get videos a user reposted  | tt_get_reposted  | tt_user_reposted_api      | \-                      |
| get pinned videos of users  | tt_get_pinned    | tt_user_pinned_videos_api | \-                      |
| get videos in a playlist    | tt_playlist      | tt_playlist_api           | \-                      |
| build query objects         | query            | (query_and, query_or, query_not) | \-               |
| get raw post data           | tt_json          | \-                        | tt_request_hidden       |
| retrieve last query/results | last_query, last_comments | \-               | \-                      |
| authenticate a session      | \-               | auth_research             | auth_hidden             |

: Function overview of `traktok` {#tbl-overview}

# Installation

The package can be installed from CRAN [@cran]:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("traktok")
```

For the development version, it is also possible to install the package from GitHub directly^[<https://github.com/JBGruber/traktok>].

# Research API

To get access to TikTok's Research API, researchers must be eligible^[The terms are available on TikTok's website for developers at <https://developers.tiktok.com/products/research-api>.], create a developer account and then apply for access to the research API with a specific research proposal.
If approved, researchers receive a client key and client secret, accessible on their developer account^[More information is provided by TikTok at <https://developers.tiktok.com/research>.].
`traktok` facilitates authentication and stores an encrypted token, which is automatically renewed when going stale (i.e., expires).
All the user has to do is run the command below once, which starts a guided process.
Through the use of `askpass` [@askpass], the client key and secret are not stored in the `R` history or any script, but outside the working directory in the user's cache.
That should make it impossible to accidentally upload confidential credentials to cloud storage or a version control system like Git.
This process usually does not have to be repeated, except when the user requests a client key or secret change from TikTok.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(traktok)
auth_research()
```

![Screenshot of authentication in the RStudio IDE](media/authentication-rstudio.png){#fig-askpass width=60%}

The most useful endpoint that the Research API offers is to search the platform for posts.
For queries, TikTok uses a fine-grained, yet complicated query syntax.^[See <https://developers.tiktok.com/doc/research-api-specs-query-videos#query>.]
For convenience, a query in `traktok` is constructed internally when you search with a key phrase directly:

```{r}
tt_query_videos("#rstats", max_pages = 2L)
```

This will match a supplied keyword or phrase against keywords and hashtags and return up to 200 results (each page has 100 results and 2 pages are requested by default) from ten and eleven days ago (the defaults are `start_date = Sys.Date() - 11` and `end_date = Sys.Date() - 10`).
This somewhat odd default window is deliberate, as TikTok states that new videos take up to 48 hours to be added to the search engine behind the Research API and that statistics such as the view count can take up to 10 days to update.^[See <https://developers.tiktok.com/doc/research-api-faq>.]
@entrena-serrano_tiktoks_2025 found in their tests that videos were frequently still missing after 72 hours, so when setting the dates manually, I recommend leaving a gap of at least three days between the end date of a query and the day it is run, and of ten days if the engagement statistics matter for the analysis.
Every white-space is treated as an AND operator.
To extend the retrieved range, you can set a start and end date (there is no limit on how far you can go back):


```{r}
tt_query_videos(
  "#rstats",
  max_pages = 2L,
  start_date = as.Date("2023-11-01"),
  end_date = as.Date("2023-11-29")
)
```

The API itself only accepts a start and end that are a maximum of 30 days apart, but `traktok` takes care of this in the background: longer time spans are split into consecutive windows of at most 30 days, which are queried one after the other before the results are combined.
The returned object also carries the start and end date of the last window as attributes, so that a search can be picked back up where it stopped more easily.

As said, the query syntax that TikTok uses is a little complicated, as users can chain queries with `AND`, `OR` and `NOT` operators (see @tbl-boolean) on a number of fields (`"create_date"`, `"username"`, `"region_code"`, `"video_id"`, `"hashtag_name"`, `"keyword"`, `"music_id"`, `"effect_id"`, and `"video_length"`).

| Operator | Results are returned if...                 |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| AND      | ...all specified conditions are met        |
| OR       | ...any of the specified conditions are met |
| NOT      | ...the specified conditions are not met    |

: Boolean operators as used by TikTok {#tbl-boolean}

To make queries easier to use, `traktok` uses a tidyverse-style approach to building a search.
For example, to get to the same query we used above, which matches #rstats against keywords and hashtags, you need to build the query like this:


```{r}
query() |> # start by using query()
  query_or(
    field_name = "hashtag_name", # add an OR condition on the hashtag field
    operation = "IN", # value should be IN list of hashtags
    field_values = "rstats"
  ) |> # hashtag field does not accept the #-symbol
  query_or(
    field_name = "keyword", # add another OR condition
    operation = "IN",
    field_values = "#rstats"
  )
```


| Operation | Results are returned if field_values are...     |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| EQ        | equal to the value in the field                 |
| IN        | equal to a value in the field                   |
| GT        | greater than the value in the field             |
| GTE       | greater than or equal to the value in the field |
| LT        | lower than the value in the field               |
| LTE       | lower than or equal to the value in the field   |

: Condition operators as used by TikTok {#tbl-match}

If #rstats is found in either the hashtag or keywords of a video, that video is then returned.
Besides checking for `EQ`ual, users can also use one of the other operations shown in @tbl-match.
This makes building queries relatively complex, but allows for fine-grained searches in the TikTok data:


```{r}
search_df <- query() |>
  query_and(
    field_name = "region_code",
    operation = "IN",
    field_values = c("JP", "US")
  ) |>
  query_or(
    field_name = "hashtag_name",
    operation = "EQ", # rstats is the only hashtag
    field_values = "rstats"
  ) |>
  query_or(
    field_name = "keyword",
    operation = "IN", # rstats is one of the keywords
    field_values = "rstats"
  ) |>
  query_not(
    operation = "EQ",
    field_name = "video_length",
    field_values = "SHORT"
  ) |>
  tt_search_api(
    start_date = as.Date("2023-11-01"),
    end_date = as.Date("2023-11-29")
  )

search_df
```

This will return videos posted in the US or Japan that have "rstats" as the only hashtag or as one of the keywords and have a length of `"MID"`, `"LONG"`, or `"EXTRA_LONG"`.^[
See <https://developers.tiktok.com/doc/research-api-specs-query-videos#condition_fields> for possible values of each field.
]

Instead of searching for videos by keyword or hashtag, the endpoint also allows querying all videos a specific account has posted:

```{r}
query() |>
  query_and(
    field_name = "username",
    operation = "EQ",
    field_values = "abdulelsayed"
  ) |>
  tt_search_api(
    start_date = as.Date("2026-11-01"),
    end_date = as.Date("2026-11-06")
  )
```

As this is a common task, `traktok` also provides the convenience function `tt_user_videos_api`, which builds this query in the background and only needs a username and, optionally, a start and end date; I use it in the section on combining the APIs below.

The second useful function that we are highlighting here is `tt_comments_api`.
Using a video ID, it retrieves the full text of user comments, along with useful information about the discussion structure, like and reply counts.

```{r}
tt_comments_api(video_id = "7705183301014654239")
```

For many research projects, it will also be of value to determine who a user follows and who they are followed by.
This can be accomplished as shown below:


```{r}
tt_user_follower_api("abdulelsayed", max_pages = 1) # 1 is the default

tt_user_following_api("abdulelsayed", max_pages = 1) # 1 is the default
```

As @tbl-overview shows, there are several other functions that query the Research API. However, `tt_user_liked_videos_api` and `tt_user_pinned_videos_api` query information that is opt-in and therefore turned off by the large majority of accounts;
`tt_playlist_api` relates to a feature of the platform that is not widely used;
and `tt_user_info_api` only returns very basic information about accounts that is usually not meaningful for research.

Importantly, a crucial part of the data, namely the video files themselves, is not accessible through the Research API --- even though videos can be downloaded through the official TikTok app.
However, `traktok` users can instead obtain this data through the 'hidden' API, discussed in the next section.

# 'Hidden' API

The unofficial or 'hidden' API is essentially what the TikTok website uses to display content.
How these endpoints work was discovered through reverse engineering --- that is, studying how the browser retrieves data to display it and mimicking this behaviour in `R`^[The groundwork for this was done by Deen Freelon and his pyktok Python package.] --- and TikTok might change how these endpoints operate at any moment.
Nevertheless, the approach has been working since 2022, with only minor adaptations of the code.

![Usage of browser cookies](media/cookies.png){#fig-cookie}

All functions of the 'hidden' API operate by utilizing the cookies stored in the browser by the website, allowing requests from `R` to mimic those from a browser for authentication purposes.
HTTP cookies are small blocks of data websites store in the browser to identify users, which can range from simple things like remembering your language preference or items in your shopping cart to more critical functions like keeping you logged in to your account by storing an authentication token that verifies your identity with each page you visit.
To get these cookies into `R`, users can log into their TikTok account (or create a new one) with a browser on their computer and then use tools like [*Get cookies.txt*](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/get-cookiestxt-locally/cclelndahbckbenkjhflpdbgdldlbecc) for Chromium-based browsers or [*cookies.txt*](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/cookies-txt/) for Firefox^[As almost all browsers used today are based on one of these, these two suggestions should satisfy all users.].
@fig-cookie shows how the process works in the browser.
It does not matter if the user downloads all cookies or just the ones specific to TikTok, as I use the `cookiemonster` package [@cookiemonster] to store cookies securely and `traktok` sends only the appropriate cookies with its requests.
To read the cookies into a specific encrypted file, a user only has to run the following command once:

```{r}
#| eval: false
auth_hidden("tiktok.com_cookies.txt")
```

A few things about these cookies are worth clarifying.
A logged-in account is not strictly necessary, as TikTok also sets cookies for visitors who are not logged in, but the website hides some content, such as age-restricted videos, from these sessions and prompts a login after a few dozen search results at most, which is why I recommend logging in before exporting the cookies.
Since the cookies identify the account uniquely, TikTok could in principle link the requests made by `traktok` to it.
As of writing, there are no known incidents of TikTok taking action against the account of a `traktok` user, but I still recommend that users rely on throwaway accounts; I return to the legal side of this in the section on legal and ethical considerations below.

Like in the Research API, users are able to search for videos, albeit at a slower pace and only within the range of what would be shown in the search on the website.
Technically, the function opens a browser in the background and keeps scrolling down until there are no more videos found or until a predefined end time is reached.
One caveat is that TikTok usually interrupts the scrolling with a CAPTCHA at some point, which is why the example below sets `solve_captchas = TRUE`; I explain what happens in that case in the section on combining the APIs below.
In the example below, we search for the hashtag "rstats" again and let the function scroll for two minutes.
It is also possible to scroll for an infinite time, stopping only when no more videos are returned.
However, whether or not an end time is defined, the user can always cancel the process without losing data.
After the function stopped or was stopped, the URLs of the videos found by the previous search can still be retrieved with `last_query()`.

```{r}
rstats_videos <- tt_search_hidden(
  "#rstats",
  scroll = "2minutes", # stop scrolling after 2 minutes
  solve_captchas = TRUE # open a browser window if a captcha is detected
)
head(rstats_videos)
head(last_query())
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# the chunks below read the search results from a file, as one would in a
# project; this file is the search from above
saveRDS(rstats_videos, "search_results.rds")
```

As with the Research API, we can once again also query the videos posted by a specific user account.
Like `tt_search_hidden`, `tt_user_videos_hidden` scrolls down the account's page in a browser in the background, so the same considerations about the scrolling time and CAPTCHAs apply, and then collects the data of all posts it found.
As the website offers no way to filter by date, the function cannot be limited to a time window like the Research API example above; instead, it starts with the most recent posts and works backwards in time until the scrolling time is up or the first post of the account is reached:

```{r}
abdulelsayed_videos <- tt_user_videos_hidden(
  "abdulelsayed",
  scroll = "2minutes", # stop scrolling after 2 minutes
  solve_captchas = TRUE # open a browser window if a captcha is detected
)
head(abdulelsayed_videos)
```

Besides their videos, we can also retrieve who follows an account and whom it follows.
The first step is to find out the internal ID of a user:

```{r}
abdulelsayed_info <- tt_user_info_hidden("abdulelsayed")
```

The important piece of information is stored in the column `secUid`, which we can hand to the `tt_get_follower_hidden` or `tt_get_following_hidden` function:

```{r}
abdulelsayed_following <- tt_get_following_hidden(abdulelsayed_info$secUid)
nrow(abdulelsayed_following)
```

For large accounts, this does not deliver the full set of followers or followed accounts, but only what would be visible on the web version (the function returns at most 5,000 accounts).
It additionally takes much longer than the Research API version.
Therefore, running the function is only interesting for researchers who do not have access to the official API.

The most important feature of the 'hidden' API, however, which is interesting also for users who already have access to the Research API, is to query information about specific posts and to download the videos or images included in them.
This is implemented in the `tt_videos` function:


```{r}
# this comes from a previously saved search
rstats_df <- readRDS("search_results.rds")
rstats_df2 <- tt_videos(rstats_df$video_url[1:2], save_video = TRUE)

rstats_df2
```

When users are scraping many URLs, which in my experience means thousands rather than hundreds, the function often fails eventually for one reason or another.
It therefore usually makes sense to save progress in a cache directory:

```{r}
rstats_df3 <- tt_videos(rstats_df$video_url[5:6], cache_dir = "rstats")

list.files("rstats")
```

With this, the package comfortably handles the scale of most research projects, which I would put somewhere between a handful and around a hundred thousand videos.
I have tested the functions with collections of about twenty thousand videos, which takes some time, and larger collections are possible with patience, but industrial-scale scraping of the platform is not what `traktok` is intended for.

Note that the video files are downloaded into your working directory by default^[Can be controlled with the `dir` argument in `tt_videos`.], independently of the cache directory.
`tt_videos` already retrieves some information that is otherwise not available, like the `video_status`, which shows a reason when a video is no longer available.
If there is information that users feel is missing from the `data.frame` that `tt_videos` returns, they can also access the raw, unparsed JSON data using:

```{r}
rstats_list1 <- tt_request_hidden(rstats_df$video_url[1]) |>
  jsonlite::fromJSON()
```

Parsing the result into a list using `fromJSON` results in a complex nested list, which users can explore further.
At the time of writing, this list contains, for example, the text of stickers placed on the video, an indicator whether the post is an advertisement, links to automatically generated subtitles, the follower count of the author and a label for AI-generated content, none of which are part of the parsed `data.frame` yet.
These fields are candidates to be added to the output of `tt_videos` in upcoming versions, as I extend the parser whenever fields turn out to be useful for research.
I refrain from documenting the raw data in more detail, however, as TikTok keeps changing which fields are available.


# Combining the APIs

As the TikTok Research API does not deliver video or image files, any analysis of the content of posts requires an alternative route to accessing these data.
`traktok` enables this access via the function `tt_videos_hidden`.
As an example for combining both APIs, let's say we want to acquire all posts from "abdulelsayed", the campaign account of American politician, epidemiologist, and academic Abdul El-Sayed, who was elected US Senator in 2026, from the days around the election (1 to 6 November 2026).
We can first search for post URLs using the Research API:

```{r}
abdulelsayed_df <- tt_user_videos_api(
  username = "abdulelsayed",
  since = "2026-11-01",
  to = "2026-11-06"
)
```

And then download the video and image files through `tt_videos_hidden`:

```{r}
results_df <- tt_videos_hidden(
  abdulelsayed_df$video_id,
  save_video = TRUE,
  cache_dir = "abdulelsayed",
  dir = "abdulelsayed",
  slideshows = TRUE
)

list.files("abdulelsayed") |>
  tools::file_ext() |>
  table()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
abdulelsayed_files <- tools::file_ext(list.files("abdulelsayed"))
```

As can be seen, the function downloaded `r sum(abdulelsayed_files == "mp4")` video files and additionally `r sum(abdulelsayed_files == "jpeg")` image files, which are now also often shared on the platform, copying one of Instagram's main features.
These image files belong to so-called slideshows or photo posts, for which TikTok has recently stopped including the data in the page source that `tt_videos_hidden` reads.
`traktok` therefore recognises slideshows among the URLs and, once all other posts are collected, asks whether to hand them to `tt_slideshow_hidden` (or does so directly with `slideshows = TRUE`), which opens each post in a browser in the background, waits until the site has requested the post data itself and collects the metadata and images from there.
As the audio track is often as important for understanding these posts as the images, the function also downloads the music of a slideshow as an mp3 file next to the images.
Since the cache was set to the same folder, we also get the raw data as JSON files.
This has the side effect that already downloaded data is not requested again, if we rerun the function, for example, with an extended list of video IDs.

The second important use case for combining both APIs is to compare them to assess the completeness of results, as has been done for Facebook [@hofacebook2020] and Twitter [@tromble_twitter_2017] in the past.
As mentioned in the introduction, Germany's far-right party AfD has managed to build a hard-to-overlook presence on TikTok, and serves as a demonstration case here.
For this, we can use the convenience function `tt_user_videos_api` mentioned above, which makes queries to the Research API for all videos a user has published:

```{r}
#| eval: false
results_api <- tt_user_videos_api(
  username = "afdfraktionimbundestag",
  since = "2020-01-01"
)
```

Its counterpart for the 'hidden' API is `tt_user_videos_hidden`, which we already used above:

```{r}
#| eval: false
results_scraping <- tt_user_videos_hidden(
  username = "afdfraktionimbundestag",
  solve_captchas = TRUE,
  scroll = Inf
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
results_api <- readRDS("afd-comparison/results_api.rds")
results_scraping <- readRDS("afd-comparison/results_scraping.rds")
results_api <- results_api |>
  mutate(video_id = as.character(video_id)) |>
  distinct(video_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(available_on_api = TRUE)
results_scraping <- results_scraping |>
  mutate(video_id = as.character(video_id)) |>
  distinct(video_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(available_on_web = TRUE)
diff_df <- results_api |>
  full_join(results_scraping, by = "video_id") |>
  mutate(
    available_on = case_when(
      available_on_api & available_on_web ~ "both",
      available_on_web ~ "website",
      available_on_api ~ "api"
    )
  )
```

This will open a real browser in the background that scrolls down on a specific account site until the beginning of a user's timeline is reached.
This process will often trigger so-called *CAPTCHA*s, which are small challenges created to test if a human or bot is performing an action on the site.
If that happens, and the argument `solve_captchas` is true, the browser will jump to the foreground, so that a user can solve it and `traktok` can continue scrolling.

Comparing the results from the Research API and the scraping effort, we see some discrepancies.
The Research API delivered `r nrow(results_api)`, while the 'hidden' API found `r nrow(results_scraping)` posts.
However, the content is also not as similar as these numbers suggest.
`r sum(diff_df$available_on == "website")` posts were only accessible via the website, while `r sum(diff_df$available_on == "api")` posts were found by the API, but not actually present on the website.
Searching manually for the videos not present on the channel page on the website, it turns out that these videos were restricted by TikTok as they contain extreme or age-restricted content --- which can also be obtained through the 'hidden' API by logging in as an age-verified user.
We currently do not know why the search from the API is incomplete (I come back to this in the final section).


# Legal and ethical considerations

Studying TikTok comes with some important legal and ethical considerations, which researchers should keep in mind.
First, when collecting data via APIs or web scraping, researchers must navigate data privacy regulations, particularly the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in Europe and similar frameworks globally which protect personal data of users [@european_union_regulation_2016].
As posts on TikTok often contain such personal data, `traktok` users usually need to familiarize themselves with what they can and cannot do with the data they obtain.
One option to legally acquire and share the data would be to obtain informed consent from the persons who appear in posts [@breuer_overview_2025].
Yet, collecting public data in bulk makes individual consent impractical [@ohme_digital_2024].
There are certain exceptions for research on systemic risks, which mandate additional requirements for the research pipeline, especially data minimization principles though --- that is, collecting only data necessary for addressing specific research questions [@breuer_overview_2025].
Preprocessing steps to remove personally identifiable information before analysis are essential [@ohme_digital_2024], though even seemingly anonymous data like follower counts with timestamps can enable re-identification [@williams_towards_2017].
For `traktok` users, this means deciding before the collection which of the returned fields a research question actually requires and discarding the rest: the `data.frame` returned by `tt_videos`, for instance, contains the usernames, display names and biographies of authors, which many analyses do not need, and the cache directory and the downloaded video files contain the complete, unprocessed data, which should be stored securely and deleted once they have served their purpose.

Secondly, platform-centric methods like scraping public content operate in a legally ambiguous space: while cases like *hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn* in the United States have upheld the legality of scraping publicly accessible data without breaching technological barriers [@ratswd_big_2020], researchers must still try to respect platform Terms of Service and consider that users may not be aware their public data can be used for research [@breuer_overview_2025].
The two ways of accessing TikTok described above differ in this respect: the Research API is an official channel, whose terms researchers accept when they apply for access, whereas the 'hidden' API needs to be considered scraping, and TikTok's Terms of Service prohibit extracting data from the platform with automated software that TikTok has not approved.^[See the section "What you can't do on the Platform" in the terms for the European Economic Area, <https://www.tiktok.com/legal/page/eea/terms-of-service/en>; the terms for the United States, <https://www.tiktok.com/legal/page/us/terms-of-service/en>, contain the same clause.]

@brown_web_2025 review the case law for the United States and conclude that the legal risk is lowest when researchers collect only what is publicly accessible without an account and do not circumvent technical barriers, and that it is higher when data are collected through an account, as the 'hidden' API functions of `traktok` can do, since the account holder has agreed to the terms and the platform can withdraw its permission at any time, for example by blocking the account.
A breach of the Terms of Service alone is not a criminal offence in the United States and the platform would have to demonstrate actual harm, which is difficult in the case of non-commercial research [@brown_web_2025], but even though unlikely, legal dispute is costly and, as @brown_web_2025 point out, a university's legal department represents the university rather than the individual researcher.

I therefore recommend that users consult their institution's legal counsel and data protection officer before collecting data at scale with the 'hidden' API, and clarify at the same time whether the institution would support them should TikTok take action against them.
Zero legal risk is not attainable in this area, and excessive caution comes at the cost of research that is in the public interest [@brown_web_2025], which is why `traktok` is built to stay within what a regular user could do in a browser: the functions of the 'hidden' API wait a random interval between requests (see the `sleep_pool` argument), which keeps the pace of requests, and thereby the load on TikTok's servers, close to that of a human user, and when the site asks for a CAPTCHA, the browser is handed to the user rather than the challenge being circumvented.

Thirdly, the Digital Services Act (DSA) in the European Union introduces new provisions mandating platforms to provide data access to qualified researchers [@ausloos_researching_2021], potentially reducing dependency on platform cooperation and legally and ethically ambiguous data collection methods.
However, implementation details and enforcement mechanisms remain evolving.
Finally, researchers should consider the ethical implications of studying vulnerable populations, particularly given TikTok's young user base, and the potential harms from analyzing sensitive content without appropriate safeguards [@breuer_overview_2025].
Questions like these are what institutional ethics boards are for, and I recommend involving them early, before a collection has started, rather than after the fact [@brown_web_2025].


# Current status and future

`traktok` provides access to TikTok, a social media platform of growing societal importance, which should be systematically studied by communication researchers.
While it is not the first or only tool to do so, the combination of access through the Research API and web scraping methods in one `R` package with an easy-to-understand consistent syntax is built to encourage this research.

Several studies have used the package already to make important contributions.
In communication research, @wirz_qualitat_2023 studied the posts of news organizations on TikTok compared with the same outlets' websites and found high-quality news reporting, albeit with more focus on emotional and soft news.
Similarly, @wirz_infotainment_2025 studied Instagram and TikTok content by news companies, finding that many outlets still share high-quality news content, peppered with some more entertainment.
@hohner_analysing_2024 studied mobilization strategies of far-right groups on TikTok and found distinct communication strategies like using conspiracy narratives and anti-elitism.
@widholm_right-wing_2024 studied election campaign videos in Sweden, revealing that youth organizations had the most prominent accounts and that right-wing content resulted in more engagement.
@peterson-salahuddin_teachable_2025 found that "TikTok’s predominantly Gen-Z users engage the platform to discuss, negotiate, and put in place socially progressive norms around racism, sexism, and homophobia" (p. 430).

But also beyond communication research, the package has already been employed for important contributions.
In medicine, @blakeman_describing_2025 studied posts with health-related information on Twitter (X), Instagram, and, using `traktok`, also TikTok.
@donaldson_describing_2025 studied how especially young users discuss nicotine pouches on TikTok, with the result that many videos featured pro-tobacco themes.

The discrepancy between the Research API and the website that I showed in the section on combining the APIs also deserves a closer look, as it is not a quirk of my example but has by now been confirmed at a larger scale.
@pearson_tiktok_api_2025 audited the API against the website and likewise found publicly available videos that the API did not return, along with view counts that were, for data collected before July 2024, orders of magnitude lower than those displayed on the website and errors when filtering by username; @corso_what_2024 obtained at most 65% of the videos they requested when drawing a random sample over six years; and @entrena-serrano_tiktoks_2025 found that one in eight videos in a donated dataset of around 260,000 posts were publicly available on the website but not retrievable through the API.
TikTok has not explained these gaps, but the audits allow for informed assumptions: besides deleted and private videos, which the documentation mentions, the API withholds advertisements, videos posted by TikTok itself, everything by creators it locates in Canada and, for no apparent reason, some accounts altogether, while a share of the missing videos remains unexplained [@entrena-serrano_tiktoks_2025].
For researchers this means that the Research API should not be mistaken for a complete record and that scraping the website remains the only way to check what it delivers, which is a second reason for keeping both routes in one package.

As noted above, TikTok can change the endpoints behind the 'hidden' API at any time, and there is no guarantee that the Research API stays as it is either.
I therefore intend to keep maintaining `traktok` for the foreseeable future: development happens openly in the GitHub repository^[<https://github.com/JBGruber/traktok>], where users can report problems and contribute fixes, and stable versions are published on CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network).
Should I at some point be unable to continue this work, which I consider unlikely, I will look for a successor and hand the package over to a new maintainer or organization rather than let it go stale.
